title: A memory-information window in finite-duration quantum control
abstract: Environmental noise is a major source of decoherence and errors in quantum systems. In a non-Markovian environment, the noise has a finite correlation time, and the system can retain information about its previous interactions with the environment. Here, we investigate how such environmental memory can be observed through a finite-duration coherent quantum operation. Coherent control dynamically reshapes the stochastic coupling operator and thereby changes how two-time noise correlations affect the quantum process. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise, we show analytically that two different limits reduce the information on the correlation time. In the short-memory limit, the leading dynamics depend on the integrated-noise combination σ/τc, where σ is the noise variance and τc is the correlation time, making these parameters locally degenerate. In the long-memory limit, the stochastic field becomes quasi-static during the operation, and sensitivity to the correlation time is suppressed. Exact stochastic simulations for a driven single-qubit Xπ rotation and a two-qubit exchange gate show that independent correlation-time information becomes largest between these limits, when the environmental and control timescales are comparable. Noncommuting controls enhance this information, whereas commuting controls do not. Simulations at different gate durations tg further show that the information window approximately follows the dimensionless correlation ratio τc/tg. These results provide a timescale-matching principle for probing finite-correlation non-Markovian noise with coherent quantum control.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework to probe environmental memory in quantum systems using coherent control. By analyzing the process map's dependence on noise correlation time ($	au_c$) versus gate duration ($t_g$), the authors identify a 'memory-information window.' This window shows that optimal noise characterization occurs when the environmental and control timescales are comparable.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the finite correlation time of environmental noise (non-Markovianity) can be experimentally detected using coherent quantum control protocols.
main_result: The ability to extract information about the noise correlation time is maximized when the environmental and control timescales are comparable, defining a 'memory-information window.'
method: The authors use exact stochastic trajectory calculations and analyze the parameter identifiability of the quantum process map by examining the Jacobian matrix of the process evolution.
model_or_system: The system involves quantum control operations (e.g., single-qubit rotations, two-qubit gates) subjected to non-Markovian environmental noise, modeled using the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.
key_observables: Process map elements, Pauli-transfer matrix (PTM) elements, and the smallest singular value of the process Jacobian.
important_parameters: Noise variance ($\sigma^2$), correlation time ($	au_c$), and gate duration ($t_g$), analyzed via the dimensionless ratio $	au_c/t_g$.
main_assumptions: The noise is modeled as Gaussian noise with a finite correlation time, and the analysis relies on the concept of independent parameter identifiability.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time-ordered dressing of stochastic interactions, showing the memory-information window, and comparing information observability for different control types (commuting vs. noncommuting).
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework for noise-induced process evolution, analyzes the short-memory and long-memory limits, and uses stochastic simulations to pinpoint the optimal timescale matching for information extraction.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, measurable principle—the timescale-matching principle—for designing quantum experiments to characterize complex, realistic noise environments beyond simple Markovian assumptions.
